Edenvale Cops

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
horrific tales of racial abuse and assault on Edenvale residents at the hands of the police

Summary:
White residents of Edenvale are routinely stopped, harassed, arrested and then assaulted by policemen on patrol. We speak to 3 such case studies who managed to capture their attackers on video. All 3 attacks were carried out by the same cops.

Further information:
Despite several complaints made to the SAPS, the Hawks and IPID, the Edenvale police seem to be a law unto themselves.

Extra Budget Items:
Retrieving video footage deleted from a cellphone by the SAPS
Surveillance of patrols.

Press Release:


Bullies in blue:
Terrified East Rand residents tell horror stories of racial abuse and assault at the hands of police. Motorists are routinely stopped, harassed, arrested and then assaulted by policemen on patrol, often for no valid reason. A fairly unique physical feature has led to repeated identification of one of the officers, and some of the victims have even managed to capture their attackers on video. But despite this evidence and several complaints to the SAPS and the Hawks, these rogue policemen continue their reign of terror. Carte blanche investigates.


Script:


EDENVALE COPS

Text: 24 December 2013
1.00am

V/O: Twenty-four year-old Darren Kingsley had been watching football at a sports bar and was heading home in his Dad’s delivery van. He had just passed the Edenvale police station when he was pulled over.

Darren: And this cop gets out the police van with his gun out and he’s pointing it towards us and telling us to get out and get on the floor.

Bongani: Had you been drinking?

Darren: No, I’m strongly religious so alcohol’s not part of my religion.

V/O; After searching them and the car he told them they were under arrest.

Darren: He tried to force us into the van so we asked him why are you arresting us? And he proceeded to shake us around, pull us around, push us, choke us and hit us on the chest.

Link: The legacy of police brutality is something we associate with the days of apartheid, and for most of us the idea of officers taunting and terrorizing citizens – especially because of the race – is all in the past right? Or is it?

Darren: He then got really aggressive with us and said I’m going to teach you White boys a lesson. I’m going to teach you f-ing White boys a lesson. He tried to get our phones off us, he said it was dangerous to him.

Bongani: Did he take your phone?

Darren: Ja, ja he forcefully removed all our phones.

V/O; They were then driven the police station, and charged with reckless and negligent driving. Darren’s father Peter waited at the station for hours before his son was released from the holding cells.

Peter: He told us quite clearly that he’d been asking for the identification of the officers because they never had their nametags on.

Bongani: Did you see any injuries?

Peter: We could see that he had a bruise on his neck.

V/O; Darren was examined by a doctor that day who filled out a J88 report. This clearly shows the bruising and abrasions that he suffered during the arrest.

Darren: Nothing of a serious nature. Just me with my shoulders – my rotary cuffs, he pulled them out.

Bongani: Why didn’t you lay a charge?

Darren: We didn’t lay a charge because the lawyer instructed us, rather just let it go away.

Bongani: What do you think would have happened if you had laid a charge?

Darren: My case would be opened again, because it’s still a pending investigation.

V/O: The Kinglsey’s went to the local paper, but nothing seemed to change.

Bongani: Have you been intimidated since the incident?

Darren: We’ve had police drive up and down the road. It happened for about a full two months after I was arrested.

Bongani: How did that make you feel?

Darren: You see them you instantly just freak out. Because you’re petrified that that they could just arrest you any time and take you away.

Text: 29 March 2014
1.15am

V/O: The next complainant is still so petrified that he only agreed to tell his story if we protect his identity. John and his wife were pulled over near the Greenstone Mall. A security camera captured the incident.

John: They asked if I’d been drinking? I said no. They asked me to climb out of the car. As I climbed out the vehicle they asked me for my drivers license. When I put my hand behind my back to get my wallet out my pocket, the first handcuff was already on.

V/O: His wife started to film the incident on her cellphone, but the policeman grabbed the phone from her and deleted the video.

John: They then put me into the back of the police vehicle, said they’re arresting me for drunken driving. There was no questions asked, there was no test, they never got to see my license. I hadn’t been drinking.

V/O: They sped off to the Edenvale Police station leaving his wife in the car. She followed them to the station, and from there to Edenvale Hospital.

Darren: They dragged me out of the vehicle, took me straight into the emergency ward. They closed all the doors behind me and everything. At this stage is when the threats started.

Bongani: What sort of things were they saying to you?

John: I’m a rich White boy and I shouldn’t be here. They will take it away from me. They still threatened my life. They said tonight I will die. They said by the end of tonight you will have AIDS.

Link: To test John’s blood alcohol levels he was brought here to the Edenvale Hospital. This is where the assault happened. A hospital is a place of safety, a place of healing. It’s the last place you’d expect to be tortured.

John: They started by hitting me in the stomach. They still moved a gent who was lying on a bed out of the way so he couldn’t see. They started hitting me in the ribs, same thing it hurt a bit more. You could see the frustration in their face, the more they were hitting me and the less I was doing. I’ll never forget the nurse still stood there and laughed at me.

V/O: The policemen then moved John to reception where he had to give all his details to hospital staff. By this time his wife had arrived and was filming them with her cellphone. When they realized what she was doing the one officer came over and snatched the phone away to delete the evidence.

Sfx: Can I have my cellphone?

No don’t argue, just step away.

John: A little while later they put me back into the emergency, this polystyrene box arrives with two red tags on it, this is supposed to be the alcohol test. This little polystyrene box disappears. A little while later another one arrives, no tags on it, no nothing and this is when he repeated it again, that you will have AIDS tonight. The one gent still pinned me down while the nurse took the blood. This is when I started to fight back and this is when they figured out that if they hit me in the back I drop like a ton a of bricks. That’s when they went to town on me. There are still photos where you can see a perfect knuckle mark in my ribcage and my spine.

V/O: John was charged with resisting arrest and drunk driving and spent the night in the cells at Edenvale Police station. He was released on bail in the morning, and was examined by a doctor who filled in a J 88 report. He also went for regular HIV tests.

Bongani: How badly were you hurt?

John: The damage they’ve done will last forever.. I was told I will never be able to lift my child.

V/O: A disc in his lower back was damaged.

Bongani: Did you lay a charge?

John: I was too scared. Before they let me out of the police station they still recited my address back to me and said that if you ever take this further we will come for you and your family. They’re not a police force, more like a gang.

Bongani: Did you get their names?

John: Nothing.

Bongani: But you would recognize them anywhere?

John: Yes, the one gentleman still had a gold tooth, as clear as day I saw that in my face a number of times.

V/O: John contacted Darren Kingsley through the local newspaper, and managed to show him the video taken at the hospital.

Darren: I know that officer. I know what he looks like. And I know that he’s capable of doing that. And it doesn’t stop at me, he can do it to other people.

V/O: And many other people have complained to the local CPF, says Chairperson Linda McKenzie.

Linda: We have no less than possibly five, six complaints a month.
We have a hundred and sixty eight police officers at Edenvale, there's only a handful that we know are doing this type of thing.

Peter: How come is it that we hear time and time and time again of these brutal arrests and the same name keeps coming up: the officer with the gold tooth, the officer with the gold tooth.

V/O: We asked the Station Commander of Edenvale Colonel Eddie Trollip about these reports.

Eddie: The CPF came forward and said it’s a policeman with gold teeth. Now I have on each shift there’s police members with gold teeth.

Bongani: How many officers have gold teeth here?

Eddie: At this stage I’m guessing but there’s at least 8 or 9 officers with gold teeth.

Bongani: It’s also alleged that in two of the incidents there were racial insults that were thrown.

Eddie: I cannot comment, but if it’s true it’s unacceptable.

Candice: It sounds to me that you either have a vigilante, racist police officer who is on his own vendetta, and then tries to cover it up by charging the individuals with these bogus charges, or you really have a lack of discipline in that particular administration.

V/O: Candice Pillay is an attorney who runs the Police Brutality Legal Clinic for ProBono.Org

Candice: The only time a police officer feels he can do something is if he can get away with it.

V/O: But in April this year the gold-toothed bully picked on the wrong guy. Gareth Williams and his wife were parked beside the road waiting for a friend at the Ridgeway bar, when officers told them to get out of the car.

Gareth: And then I started shouting for the other patrons to come closer, just to see what was going on, and the guy pushed me. And as he pushed me, I took my hands between his two hands, and I pushed his hands away, and I said, don’t you fucking touch me. You have no right to touch me. With no conversation whatsoever, the taller police officer put my hands behind my back, put handcuffs on, and threw me in the back of the van.

V/O: When they arrived at the police station they took Gareth through to an area near the reception cells.

Gareth: I’m walking in front of both the police officers and he just grabbed me and threw me into, like a wooden bench. He said go and stand over there. So I went and stood right next to a waiting cell. One of the police officers, the smaller of the two, started talking my laces out of my shoes, and my belt. And as he was doing that, I just felt this big smash on my face. I still had my hands behind my back. I came round again, he hit me again. And as I sat down, I put my head between my legs, just to protect my face, and as I did that, he hits me in the ribs. When he hit me in the ribs, I automatically popped up again, and he hit me in the face. I can’t even tell you how many times he punched me in the arms. And the comments he was making. You’re clever now...you want to call us motherfuckers. And he was just going off.

V/O: Gareth was charged with crimen injuria, resisting arrest and assaulting a police officer. At his first court appearance he was able to get a copy of the docket which contained the name of the arresting officer Constable Derick Mapatlare. This is the same name that appears on John’s charge sheet.

Bongani: Would you recognize the officer that assaulted you?

Gareth: Yes, yes.

Bongani: Were there any identifying features?

Gareth: Gold tooth. Straight away, the taller guy has a gold tooth.

V/O: Gareth has now laid a charge of assault against Constable Mapatlare. We confronted the man with the golden tooth at Edenvale police station. He had no answer to the allegations and meekly led us inside to his commanding officer. We showed Colonel Trollip the hospital video.

Bongani: Do you recognize the smaller officer, the shorter one?

Eddie: No, I cannot see the face properly.

V/O: But Carte Blanche’s involvement has triggered some action.

Bongani: Have you asked Derick Mapatlare about these cases?

Eddie: I’ve warned him yes. I said there’s a departmental investigation to be done against him. What we will do is approach all these people who is willing to come forward and give statements.

Bnngani: They say they were threatened by these officers who told them we know where you live?

Eddie: If a police member threatens anyone it is a criminal offence. He cannot do that. To keep quiet and to stay away is not going to help us you know.

Candice: Fear is what assisted apartheid to go on for so long, and I think people actually need to take a stand against corruption and bad behavior by police officers.

V/O: But Gareth found this incident so traumatic that he’s decided to emigrate.

Gareth: I resigned from my job because obviously we’re leaving and...the sooner the better. The last blanket of security that we have in this country is the SAPS and I don’t feel secure.
